questions.q: Why do forensic investigators work from the outside in rather than starting at the source?
a: Starting at the source can bias you and make you miss evidence
Evidence at the edges is always easier to collect
Labs can only process samples taken from the outside
Courts require evidence to be gathered in a set order
questions.why: The firecracker example shows that assuming the whole picture up front leads investigators to stop looking too early.

questions.q: How were fingerprints first noticed as a useful way to identify people?
a: A doctor saw potters' marks on ancient clay fragments
A prison guard compared the hands of inmates
A chemist studied ink stains left on letters
A photographer spotted marks on glass plates
questions.why: The second lesson describes Henry Faulds noticing marks on pottery in Japan and dusting them with powder.

questions.q: What did Henry Faulds do with his fingerprint idea?
a: He passed it to Charles Darwin, who sent it to Francis Galton
He opened the first fingerprint bureau at Scotland Yard
He published a book arguing against the method
He sold his notes to an Argentinian prison
questions.why: The summary traces the idea from Faulds to Darwin to Galton, before it reached India and Scotland Yard.

questions.q: Why are missing children especially hard to identify from photographs?
a: Their faces are not fully formed, so they are hard to tell apart
Photographs of children are usually too blurry
Children deliberately change how they look
Records are rarely kept for young children
questions.why: The third lesson says only one in six missing children is found through photo identification for this reason.

questions.q: What does facial reconstruction use to derive a victim's features?
a: The 22 bones of the human skull
A database of family photographs
Dental records and hair samples
Witness descriptions of the victim
questions.why: The third lesson explains that CT scans and X-rays of the skull's 22 bones let computers rebuild a face.
